newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope and Carey hold ground on divisive issues.
newsitem.headline: Pope and Carey hold ground on divisive issues.

text.p: Pope John Paul and Archbishop of Canterbury George Carey held their ground on Thursday on issues dividing their Catholic and Anglican Churches, each asking the other to understand his position.

In formal speeches after 35 minutes of closed talks in the Pope's private study, neither leader specifically mentioned the thorny question of women priests. But both made clear references to it when they spoke of recent obstacles on the path to unity.
"Sadly, these difficulties seem to loom large on the way to the reconciliation which (a 30-year theological) dialogue intended to promote," the Pope told Carey.

The 76-year-old Polish Pontiff, who later asked Carey to change his programme and stay for lunch, asked Anglicans to "reflect on the motives and reasons of the positions I have expressed" as the successor of St Peter.

Carey told the Pope that both Churches, which split in 1534 over the issue of papal authority, were now called on "to reaffirm the integrity of the other, knowing that decisions will be made that we ourselves find difficult".
Carey said Roman Catholic and Anglican leaders had to listen to people on both sides "whose voices call out to those in authority in the Church in tones of frustration and anxiety".
The Vatican says the Catholic Church does not have the authority to ordain women because Christ chose only men as his apostles in an act that showed divine will.
A few Anglican bishops, several hundred priests and several thousand worshippers have converted to Rome over the issue.
The first women were ordained in the Church of England, mother church of Anglicanism, in 1994, four years after Carey was elected the Communion's spiritual leader.
Carey told the Pope that, in striving for unity, leaders of both Churches should look to the year 2000 as an opportunity for "repentance" for divisive actions in past centuries.
The Pontiff and Carey were assisted by one aide each in their closed talks before making speeches for the delegations in the frescoed study where the Pope receives world leaders.
The atmosphere during the public part of the audience was very cordial. The Pope chatted amiably with Carey's wife and other members of his delegation, which included two other women.
Recognition of the Pope's supreme authority over any unified Christian Church, or papal primacy, has been another thorny issue testing the Catholic-Anglican dialogue.
The Pope said in a 1995 encyclical that, for the sake of unity, he was willing to seek an accommodation with other Christian denominations on the future role of the Papacy.

The Pope and Carey were due later on Thursday to worship together at the church of San Gregorio al Celio, from where St Augustine, the first archbishop of Canterbury, set out for England 1,400 years ago.

The Church of England was founded when King Henry VIII issued an act denying papal jurisdiction and broke with Rome over the refusal by Pope Clement VII to grant him a marriage annulment so that he could wed Anne Boleyn.
Carey is due to visit Milan on Friday before returning to Britain.
